intro: Wet room installation in Exeter typically costs between £6,000 and £12,000, depending on the size of the space, the complexity of the waterproofing, and the quality of materials you choose. That might sound like a significant outlay, but a properly installed wet room adds real value to an Exeter home — both in terms of daily usability and resale appeal. The key word there is *properly*. A wet room done badly is one of the most expensive bathroom mistakes you can make. Done well, with the right tanking, drainage, and tiling, it will last decades without a drop of water going where it shouldn't.
localContext: Exeter's housing stock throws up some interesting challenges when it comes to wet room installation. The city's Edwardian semis — particularly common in areas like St Leonard's and Heavitree — often have solid floors downstairs and timber joists upstairs, which significantly affects how drainage can be installed. Upstairs wet rooms in these properties require a particularly robust tanking system and careful attention to the floor build-up to avoid compromising the structural integrity of the joists. Post-war estate properties in parts of Pinhoe and Whipton tend to have more straightforward concrete or screed floors, which are generally more forgiving for wet room work. Exeter's newer developments, especially around Newcourt and Alphington, often have underfloor heating already in place, which can actually complement a wet room installation beautifully. It's also worth knowing that Exeter sits in a moderately hard water area, so specifying the right grout, sealant, and drainage fittings will help prevent limescale build-up and extend the lifespan of the finished installation.
serviceDetail: A wet room installation is a multi-trade project, and understanding what that involves helps you manage expectations around timescale and disruption. Most jobs in Exeter homes take between five and ten working days from start to finish, depending on complexity. The process begins with a survey of your existing bathroom — your installer will assess the floor structure, the existing waste and soil pipe positions, and the wall construction. This survey informs the drainage layout, which is central to everything else. The floor is then prepared, with a former or screed used to create the correct fall towards the drain. This is precise work — even a slight error here leads to pooling water. Next comes tanking, which is the waterproof membrane applied to walls and floor before any tiling begins. In Exeter's Edwardian properties, this stage often takes longer because original plasterwork may need to come off and walls may need re-boarding with moisture-resistant materials. Once tanking is complete and cured, tiling can begin. Most wet rooms use large-format porcelain tiles, which reduce grout lines and make cleaning easier. Plumbing connections — including the shower valve, any glass screens or panels, heated towel rails, and lighting — are fitted and tested last. Before sign-off, the entire installation should be tested for leaks, not just visually inspected.
pricing: In Exeter, a straightforward wet room conversion of a standard bathroom — around 4 to 6 square metres — typically sits between £6,000 and £8,500. Larger spaces, or those requiring significant structural preparation such as upstairs installations in Edwardian semis with timber floors, can push costs to £10,000–£12,000 or beyond. Premium materials — designer drainage channels, bespoke tiling, frameless glass screens — add to the upper end. Labour costs in Exeter are broadly in line with the South West average, though experienced wet room specialists may charge a premium over general bathroom fitters, which is usually worth paying. Always request an itemised quote.
whyLocal: Wet room installation isn't a job where you want someone learning the local quirks on your project. An Exeter-based tradesperson will have worked in the city's Edwardian semis, navigated the tight bathrooms in post-war estates, and dealt with the planning and build-up challenges that come with the area's mix of property types. They'll know local suppliers, understand typical build standards across different parts of the city, and — crucially — they're accountable. If something goes wrong six months down the line, a local installer is reachable. That matters enormously with a water-sensitive installation like a wet room.

faqs.q: Can I have a wet room installed upstairs in my Exeter Edwardian semi?
faqs.a: Yes, but it requires more preparation than a ground-floor installation. Timber joists need to be assessed for their load-bearing capacity and condition, and the drainage outlet will need to connect to your existing soil stack. A good installer will survey the floor structure first and may recommend a specialist tanking system designed specifically for timber subfloors. It's very achievable — just budget a little more time and cost.

faqs.q: How long does a wet room installation take in a typical Exeter home?
faqs.a: Most wet room installations in Exeter take between five and ten working days. Simpler conversions in modern properties or ground-floor rooms with concrete floors tend to come in at the lower end. Older properties — Edwardian semis in particular — often take longer due to floor preparation and wall re-boarding. Your installer should give you a realistic programme during the survey, not just a best-case estimate.

faqs.q: Will hard water in Exeter cause problems with my wet room over time?
faqs.a: Exeter's moderately hard water can cause limescale build-up on drainage fittings, shower heads, and around tile grout if you're not proactive about it. Using a water softener or softening shower head helps, as does choosing epoxy grout rather than standard cement grout — it's far more resistant to staining and mineral deposits. Regular cleaning with a pH-neutral product will keep the installation looking good for years.

faqs.q: Do I need planning permission for a wet room conversion in Exeter?
faqs.a: In most cases, no — converting an existing bathroom to a wet room is classed as permitted development and doesn't require planning permission. However, if you're in a listed building or a conservation area in Exeter city centre or the Cathedral Quarter, you may need to check with Exeter City Council before any structural alterations. Your installer should flag this during the initial survey if it's relevant to your property.

localParagraph: Exeter is a city of remarkable architectural variety, where Georgian townhouses in the cathedral quarter sit alongside Victorian terraces in St Thomas, post-war semis in Heavitree, and modern new-builds spreading out towards Alphington and Pinhoe. This mix of property ages and layouts means wet room installation across Exeter requires a genuinely adaptable approach, since older homes often present challenges around floor structures, drainage gradients, and original tiling substrates that newer properties simply do not. Water hardness in the region is mixed, drawing from both soft moorland sources via Dartmoor reservoirs and harder supplies blended through the wider Devon network, which influences material choices for shower valves, drainage channels, and grout compatibility over time. A professionally installed wet room accounts for these variables from the outset, ensuring waterproofing membranes, tanking systems, and gradient falls are all correctly specified for the building in question. Homeowners and landlords throughout Exeter should seek installers familiar with local property types and utility conditions to avoid costly remedial work further down the line.
